lead: The unit connects the measurable pressure, volume and temperature of a pure fluid to equations of state and generalized charts. It covers ideal-gas processes, real-gas corrections, compressibility factors and heat effects. After it, a student can estimate P, V or T, read a generalized compressibility chart, and compute sensible, latent and reaction heats.
about: The unit starts with 2.1, the shapes of P-V-T surfaces and phase diagrams for a pure fluid. 2.2 treats the ideal gas as the limiting case and works through isobaric, isochoric, isothermal, adiabatic and polytropic processes. 2.3 adds virial and cubic equations of state, especially van der Waals, to correct the ideal picture. 2.4 turns these equations into the compressibility factor and generalized correlations based on reduced properties. 2.5 uses the same property ideas for sensible heat, latent heat and heat of reaction. Each chapter uses the first law from Unit 1 and prepares for property relations, phase equilibria and reaction equilibria later.

chapters.idea: A pure fluid's phase and volumetric behaviour is read from its P-V-T surfaces and phase diagram.
chapters.depth: Cover P-V, P-T and T-V diagrams; isotherms; the saturation dome; triple point; critical point; supercritical fluid; saturated liquid and saturated vapour. For one component the phase rule is F = C - P + 2, so with C = 1: F = 3 - P; one phase has F = 2, two phases F = 1, triple point F = 0. Introduce 'mathematical representation of PVT behaviour' as a bridge: an equation of state is an algebraic relation P = f(V, T). Some syllabi call this volumetric properties of pure fluids. Only a few universities teach the statistical-mechanical link from intermolecular potential to phase behaviour; give it one line. Keep graphs qualitative; use water as the running example.

figure.title: Water phase diagram
figure.aria: A pressure–temperature plot for water shows the saturation line from the triple point to the critical point and three states at 1 bar: 25°C liquid, 100°C boiling and 120°C vapour.

chapters.example: For water, mark the triple point (0.01°C, 0.006 bar) and critical point (374°C, 221 bar). At 1 bar, identify the phase at 25°C, 100°C and 120°C. Answer: liquid, liquid–vapour, vapour.
chapters.trap: Treating the saturation line as a single phase, or calling the critical point a normal boiling point. At the critical point liquid and vapour become one phase.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: system, state, P, V, T, pure substance.
chapters.leave: Mixture phase diagrams and VLE to Unit 6; fugacity to Unit 5; property tables to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The ideal gas law gives simple P-V-T paths, and each path fixes work, heat and ΔU.
chapters.depth: State PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. For an ideal gas U and H depend on T only; Cv = (∂U/∂T)_V, Cp = (∂H/∂T)_P, Cp − Cv = R, γ = Cp/Cv. Work through isochoric, isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic and polytropic PVⁿ = constant processes; compute W, Q, ΔU, ΔH with a stated sign convention. Some syllabi call these non-flow processes; the flow version is in Unit 1. Mention ideal-gas mixtures only as a limiting case.

figure.title: Three ideal-gas paths
figure.aria: Pressure–volume plot for 1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K from 24.94 L: three paths to 12.47 L; the isothermal ends at 2.00 bar, the adiabatic at 2.64 bar and the isobaric stays at 1.00 bar.

chapters.example: 1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K and 1 bar has V = 24.94 L. It is taken to 12.47 L by (a) an isothermal, (b) an adiabatic (γ = 1.4) and (c) an isobaric path. Find the final pressure on each path. Answer: 2.00 bar, 2.64 bar, 1.00 bar.
chapters.trap: Using PV^γ = constant for an isothermal path, or putting T in °C into PV = nRT. Also watch sign: work done by the gas is positive in many chemistry texts but negative in many engineering texts; state the convention.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for P-V diagrams; Unit 1 for first law and enthalpy.
chapters.leave: Entropy changes and second law to Unit 3; steady-flow nozzle and compressor equations to Unit 1; real-gas deviations to Chapter 3.

chapters.idea: Virial and cubic equations of state correct the ideal gas by adding molecular size and attraction terms.
chapters.depth: Start from Z = PV/RT. Virial form: Z = 1 + B/V + C/V² + ... or Z = 1 + B'P + C'P² + ...; B is the second virial coefficient, C the third, and so on. Truncate at B for moderate pressure. Cubic form: van der Waals P = RT/(V − b) − a/V², with a = 27R²Tc²/(64Pc), b = RTc/(8Pc), and Zc = 3/8. Explain a as attraction and b as excluded volume. Name Redlich-Kwong, Soave-Redlich-Kwong and Peng-Robinson only as improved cubics; no derivation. Write the reduced van der Waals equation and the law of corresponding states as the first generalized EOS; full charts are Chapter 4. Some syllabi call this mathematical representation of PVT behaviour. Keep numerical work to one gas.

figure.title: CO₂ at 300 K: ideal vs van der Waals
figure.aria: Pressure–volume plot for 1 mol of CO₂ at 300 K: the ideal-gas curve lies above the van der Waals curve, and at 1 L the pressures are 24.94 bar and 22.41 bar.

chapters.example: For 1 mol of CO₂ at 300 K and V = 1.00 L, use R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, a = 3.640 L² bar mol⁻² and b = 0.04267 L mol⁻¹. Find P from the ideal gas law and from the van der Waals equation. Answer: 24.94 bar and 22.41 bar.
chapters.trap: Putting V instead of (V − b), mixing L with m³, or using a and b of one gas with data of another. The van der Waals equation is poor near the critical point; do not force it there.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for ideal gas; critical constants Tc and Pc.
chapters.leave: Generalized charts to Chapter 4; fugacity and residual properties to Unit 4; mixture EOS to Unit 6 or later.

chapters.idea: The compressibility factor lets one correlation cover many real gases through reduced temperature and pressure.
chapters.depth: Define Z = PV/RT; Z = 1 for an ideal gas, and deviation from 1 measures real behaviour. Define Tr = T/Tc, Pr = P/Pc, Vr = V/Vc. Principle of corresponding states: fluids at the same Tr and Pr have the same Z in a two-parameter correlation. Add the Pitzer acentric factor ω for a three-parameter correlation; Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹ with values from charts or tables, no derivation. Show how to read a generalized compressibility chart and use generalized equations of state. For gas mixtures state pseudocritical mixing rules in one line only. Some syllabi call this generalized compressibility factor correlation. Work one chart-reading example with a given Z.

figure.title: Reading a generalized chart
figure.aria: Flowchart: given T and P, look up Tc and Pc, compute Tr and Pr, read Z from a generalized chart, then calculate molar volume.

chapters.example: A gas has Tc = 300 K and Pc = 50 bar. At T = 360 K and P = 100 bar, a generalized chart gives Z = 0.65. Find Tr, Pr and the molar volume using R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Answer: Tr = 1.2, Pr = 2.0, V = 0.195 L/mol.
chapters.trap: Using T and P directly on the chart without Tc and Pc, or assuming Z = 1 at high pressure because the gas is permanent. Chart reading is approximate; keep units consistent.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3 for EOS and critical constants.
chapters.leave: Fugacity coefficients and residual properties to Unit 4; mixture VLE to Unit 6; detailed EOS forms to Chapter 3.

chapters.idea: Heat added or removed changes temperature, changes phase, or changes chemical bonds.
chapters.depth: Define sensible heat Q = ∫n Cp dT, or Q = m cp ΔT when cp is constant. Define latent heat at constant T and P. Define heat of reaction at constant P as ΔH and at constant V as ΔU, with ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT. Cover standard heat of formation, standard heat of combustion, Hess's law and Kirchhoff's law ΔH_T2 = ΔH_T1 + ∫ΔCp dT; define ΔCp. Some syllabi call this heat effects accompanying chemical reactions. Use simple constant cp values; link real-fluid enthalpies to Unit 4. Work one path from ice to steam. Do not teach the equilibrium constant.

figure.title: Enthalpy path: ice to steam
figure.aria: Enthalpy–temperature path for 1 kg of water: sensible heating of ice to 0°C, a flat fusion step, sensible heating of liquid to 100°C, a flat vaporization step, then sensible heating of steam to 120°C; total 3073 kJ/kg.

chapters.example: Heat 1 kg of ice at −10°C to steam at 120°C at 1 atm. Use cp,ice = 2.09 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔH_fus = 334 kJ kg⁻¹, cp,water = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔH_vap = 2260 kJ kg⁻¹, cp,steam = 2.01 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the total heat. Answer: 3073 kJ.
chapters.trap: Adding latent heat at the wrong temperature, or forgetting the sensible heat before and after a phase change. For a reaction, keep the sign of ΔH and note constant-pressure versus constant-volume conditions.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for enthalpy and first law; Chapter 2 for Cp and sensible heat.
chapters.leave: Reaction equilibrium and equilibrium constant to Unit 7; residual enthalpies and steam tables to Unit 4; refrigeration cycles to Unit 3.
